reasoning: 18-month-old with single episode of vomiting; no fever reported
Alert, active behavior, attempting normal play—suggests no severe distress or altered mental status
Clinical appearance reassuring: good hydration (drinking eagerly), afebrile, normal responsiveness
CRITICAL GAP: Vital signs NOT recorded—unable to assess HR, RR, BP against age-specific norms for toddler (normal HR 80–130, RR 20–30); this is a significant limitation
Vomiting alone in well-appearing toddler without fever/systemic signs does not immediately suggest sepsis, obstruction, or surgical emergency
Mother's observation of hydration status is reassuring but not a substitute for formal assessment
Likely requires ≥2 resources: labs (electrolytes, urinalysis ± CBC), imaging (abdominal ultrasound or CT if obstruction suspected), ongoing observation
Single resource (e.g., oral rehydration education alone) would underestimate risk; vomiting in toddler warrants workup
No red flags for ESI-2 (fever, severe distress, altered mental status, signs of shock) currently apparent, but absence of vitals creates uncertainty
Erring toward ESI-3 over ESI-4 acknowledges need for multiple diagnostic interventions and close monitoring in first encounter with no baseline
red_flags: Vital signs completely absent at triage—MUST be obtained immediately to rule out tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea suggestive of dehydration or occult infection
Toddler with vomiting and no prior record—cannot exclude surgical abdomen, intussusception, or early sepsis on appearance alone
Immunization status unknown—if incomplete and fever develops, meningitis/invasive bacterial disease risk rises
Age 18 months: atypical presentations common; occult dehydration and early shock can present with preserved alertness
If vomiting recurs, vital signs worsen, or lethargy emerges during ED stay → immediate re-triage to ESI-2
